## Part 1 · 00:00

[00:00] Hello. Thank you for joining me in my study. As I continue to study the role of sacrifice and the atonement in the Old Testament, it is indispensable to take account of the work of the Jewish scholar Jacob Milgrom. Milgrom is the author of a massive multi-volume commentary on the book of Leviticus. And in this commentary, he emphasizes so strongly the role of the sacrifices in purging the tabernacle and the altar and its other sacred objects of impurity that one might get the impression that this is all the sacrifices do. In fact,

[00:47] I've seen other commentators um trivialize the role of the sacrifices in removing moral guilt and sin in favor of them simply purging the tabernacle and its objects of ritual impurity. But reducing the function of the sacrifices to simply cleansing objects, I think is both implausible and doesn't do justice to the biblical text itself. Purging mere objects of impurity would leave the people themselves morally guilty and sinful and therefore would fail to address the root of the problem. It would be treating the symptom without treating the disease.

[01:33] Moreover, the text itself repeatedly makes promises such as this. The priest shall make atonement on his behalf for the sin which he has committed and he shall be forgiven. Leviticus 5:10. The word translated uh here to make atonement, kipper in the Hebrew, It a range of meanings, to purge, to ransom, to expiate. But I think what's significant here is the result. The person's sins are forgiven. The ritual sacrifice has removed his guilt.

[02:22] And so Milgrom himself advises, and I quote, "Although the cult concentrates heavily on the purging of sanctuary impurity, it too recognizes that the ultimate source of impurity is human sin." Sin must therefore be expiated. The continual purging and reconsecration of the altar, says Milgrom, "points to the singular function of the altar. It is the medium of God's salvific expiation of the sins of Israel.

[03:03] Therefore, not only does it have to be purged of Israel's sins, it must be a fit instrument for effecting expiation for Israel when sacrifices are offered upon it." He says, "For the complete annulment of sin, for the assurance of divine forgiveness, sacrificial expiation, kipper, is always required." Kipper then, in its most abstract sense, comes to mean to atone or to expiate. And Milgrom says the meaning here is the the offerer. Note, not the objects, the offerer himself is cleansed of his impurities and sins and becomes reconciled at one with God.

[03:40] This just is to say that the Old Testament sacrifices offered an atonement for sin and guilt.
